edges.effect_quant: The best pooled evidence suggests a small upward shift in breast-cancer risk with sustained night-shift exposure, with longer duration looking more concerning than short exposure.
edges.population: adult women exposed to night-shift work
edges.mechanism: Night-shift schedules can suppress melatonin, disrupt circadian regulation, and disturb sleep and metabolic timing in ways that plausibly affect hormone-responsive breast tissue. The biologic rationale is credible, but the observed epidemiologic effect is modest and not perfectly consistent across study designs.
edges.summary: The strongest evidence comes from the large prospective-cohort meta-analysis showing a small overall increase in breast-cancer incidence and a clearer signal after long-duration exposure. Other pooled studies generally point in the same direction, though not all subsets are equally convincing, so the best summary is modest harm rather than a large effect.
edges.caveats: Exposure definitions vary widely across this literature, from rotating shifts to cumulative years of night work. That heterogeneity, plus healthy-worker effects and confounding by occupation, makes the magnitude less certain than the direction.

evidence.citation: Wei F et al 2022 Sleep Breath
evidence.notes: Night-shift work, breast cancer incidence, and all-cause mortality: an updated meta-analysis of prospective cohort studies.
